It sits at its floor on bare articles, demonstratives, inanimate and accusative forms (the, a, this, that, its, which, it, him, them), and it roughly doubles when the same opener is the second or later element of a parallel or list construction ('his tuition ... and his books', 'his paternal lineage ... and his maternal lineage', the third name in a comma list).

The vessel was old but sound, and the captain, a woman of forty, had made the crossing three times before and chose the northern route despite the warnings of the harbor pilots. For the first two weeks the weather held, and the crew settled into a routine of watches, repairs, and long meals in the cramped cabin below deck. Then the wind shifted, and the sky turned the color of slate. By the third week the sea had risen, and the deck was awash with freezing spray. The cook lost two fingers to frostbite, and the carpenter spent a full night repairing a leak that opened along the keel. No one slept well after that. The fresh water began to taste of iron, and the salted meat turned gray in its barrels. Off the edge of the ice fields the vessel met a current that pushed it south for three days, and the navigator compared the charts with the stars each evening but could find no certain match. Morale thinned. Two men asked to be put ashore at the next opportunity, though no land had been sighted for weeks. The captain ordered the holds searched for the spare compass that the previous owner had described in the bill of sale, and the crew spent an afternoon moving crates and barrels by lamplight. The compass was found at last in a chest of tools, wrapped in oilcloth; the glass was cracked, but the needle still swung true. With it the navigator fixed a course along the edge of the pack, where the water stayed open and the seals lay thick on the floes. The crew hunted when the ice allowed, and the cook made a thin stew that the men ate without complaint. By the end of the fifth month the provisions were nearly gone, and the captain ordered a turn toward the southern passage, which the older charts marked with a dotted line and a note of warning. The vessel sailed for eleven days through fog so thick that the bow could not be seen from the wheel, sounding the depth every hour and listening for the surf. On the twelfth day the fog lifted, and the cliffs of the passage stood above the water like a wall. Beyond the cliffs the current carried them into a wide bay where the water was flat and green, and there the anchor was dropped for the first time in six weeks. The crew washed clothes, mended sails, and slept in the open air. The captain walked the shore alone and returned with a handful of shells and a plan to winter in the bay if the weather turned. It did not turn. When the ice finally broke in early summer, the navigator spread the charts across the table and waited while she found the first clear line of the season.

It sits at its floor on bare articles, demonstratives, inanimate and accusative forms (the, a, this, that, its, which, it, him, them), and it roughly doubles when the same opener is the second or later element of a parallel or list construction ('his tuition ... and his books', 'his paternal lineage ... and his maternal lineage', the third name in a comma list).
